findings.title: The ledger doesn't pin the per-key order of acquire, decide, and release, or what releases a key when a decision raises
findings.why_it_matters: Summary reads as acquire-all-then-decide while D1 implies per-key; neither says what releases a key when a decision raises or is cancelled, so R can behave like H and AppKeyLock claims can drift.
findings.chosen: Rewrite the Summary's Lock move bullet as strictly per-key acquire/decide/release-or-keep, released exactly once including on raise or cancel

findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a batch can wait, up to the stop deadlines, behind an in-flight HTTP action on a key whose plan comes out empty, holding its earlier restart keys and `_change_event_lock` meanwhile

findings.title: "No flag means safe to replace" ignores stops that fail before a teardown report exists
The mixed flagged-plus-live early return in `create_instances` has no test
findings.why_it_matters: The Build section says `create_instances` refuses before `load_class` when the indices are a mix of flagged and live with nothing left to create. No test pins that case. `TestAppFactoryNeedsRestartGate` covers all-flagged, flagged-plus-creatable, and flagged-plus-live-plus-creatable, but never flagged-plus-live alone. A refactor could start re-importing the module, or apply `force_reload`, for a partly flagged app whose other indices are all running, and no test would catch it.
findings.chosen: In `TestAppFactoryNeedsRestartGate`, add a test with two instances (`THREE_INSTANCES[:2]`). Index 0 is live: `mock_registry.get` returns a Mock for idx 0 and None otherwise, and `get_running_apps` returns `{0: existing_app}`. Index 1 is flagged: `flag_indices(mock_registry, 1)`. Call `create_instances("test_app", mock_manifest, force_reload=True)` and assert four things: `created == set()`, `mock_load_class.assert_not_called()`, `mock_registry.record_failure.assert_not_called()`, and exactly one ERROR equal to `record.refusal_message("test_app", 1)`. The test passes whether or not Finding 2's simplification is applied.

findings.title: `any_flagged` exists only to keep a no-op `load_class` call on all-live starts
findings.why_it_matters: "All flagged" and "all live" both mean nothing to create. Only the first returns early. The second still calls `load_class` with `force_reload` forced to False, which reads the cache and gets thrown away. That split costs a variable (`any_flagged`), a compound condition, and an `if to_create:` guard in the class-load-failure branch. Every reader of `create_instances` has to work out why the two cases differ, and the answer is that nothing depends on the difference.
findings.chosen: A: Replace the gate's exit with `if not to_create: return set()`, delete `any_flagged` and the `if to_create:` guard, flip the all-indices-occupied test to assert `load_class` is not called, and update the gate comment and the design.md:214 Build note
findings.recommended: A: Replace the gate's exit with `if not to_create: return set()`, delete `any_flagged` and the `if to_create:` guard, flip the all-indices-occupied test to assert `load_class` is not called, and update the gate comment and the design.md:214 Build note

findings.title: D1 says the accepted batch wait is bounded by stop deadlines, but a held key can be mid-start
findings.why_it_matters: D1's ratified sentence accepts that a batch can wait "up to the stop deadlines" behind an in-flight HTTP action on a no-op key. Meanwhile it holds its earlier restart keys and `_change_event_lock`, so every later file-change event queues. But the action holding that key can be an HTTP `start_app`, `start_instance`, or `reload_app` (stop then start). These are bounded by `startup_timeout` per initializing instance, not by a stop deadline. With several contended keys, the waits add up. The risk the user accepted is smaller than the real one. The wait is still finite, so this is about stating the accepted risk correctly, not about the code.
findings.chosen: A: Amend D1's `**Ratified:**` accepting clause to say the batch can wait up to the stop and startup deadlines of the action holding each contended key, adding up across keys
findings.recommended: A: Amend D1's `**Ratified:**` accepting clause to say the batch can wait up to the stop and startup deadlines of the action holding each contended key, adding up across keys

findings.title: The refusal is a lookup, a formatter that needs outside coordinates, and an ERROR, written out at both funnels
findings.why_it_matters: Each funnel calls `get_needs_restart(app_key, idx)`, branches on the result, calls `record.refusal_message(app_key, idx)`, and logs it. The record doesn't hold its own `app_key` or index, so a caller could pass a pair that doesn't match the record it looked up, and nothing would catch it. Both call sites pass matching pairs today. A registry method `refusal_for(app_key, index) -> str | None` would fold the lookup and the format into one call. The import-cycle reason the Build section gives for the method form would not apply, since `AppFactory` already holds `self.registry` and needs no import. `get_needs_restart` would stay, because `resolve_instance_info` uses it (app_registry.py:181).
findings.chosen: Side B: Replace with AppRegistry.refusal_for(app_key, index) -> str | None

findings.title: A needs-restart flag outlives the config entry it was set on
findings.why_it_matters: The gate keys on `(app_key, index)`, and `_needs_restart` is cleared only by `clear_all` (process exit or test reset). If an operator removes a flagged app, or shrinks its instance list, and later restores it, every start at that index is refused with an ERROR until hassette restarts. That is the right result if the old work is still running, and the refusal message's "flagged ... at <time>" still describes the situation. The docs already say the flag persists "even after the app is stopped or removed from the config" (operating/index.md:243) and "Only a Hassette restart clears the flag" (:253). They don't spell out that re-adding the app is refused.
findings.chosen: Side A: Add one sentence to the operating docs: removing and re-adding a flagged app doesn't clear the flag
findings.choice_reason: Asked whether the flag lives forever or a later milestone PR clears it; it is permanent until restart by design, then chose side A.

findings.title: The lock-scope unit tests can't detect a regression of decide-under-lock
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a library with many future contributors. `TestApplyChangesLockScope` pins only D1's release behavior, and the Build section says it passes on the pre-change code. If someone moves `_decide_restart` back outside the lock, only the two integration tests catch it. Those depend on timing orchestration.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: only the two integration tests guard the decide-under-lock move
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: only the two integration tests guard the decide-under-lock move

findings.title: A batch waiting on a busy key lock logs nothing
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a long-running deployment where a hung stop is possible. `apply_changes` now waits on every changed key's lock, no-op keys included, while holding `_change_event_lock` and its earlier restart keys. While it waits, config changes stop applying and nothing says why. D1 accepts the wait itself (see Finding 3 for its real bound). It doesn't address the wait being silent.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a batch waiting behind a held app-key lock logs nothing until it proceeds
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a batch waiting behind a held app-key lock logs nothing until it proceeds

findings.title: A raising decision for one key abandons the whole batch
findings.why_it_matters: If `_plan_reload` or `_should_restart` raises for key B, the restart already decided for key A is dropped, and so are the `new_apps` autostarts. A keeps running on stale config until the next save. This is not a regression. The pre-change code built every plan before `_restart_apps` and before the `new_apps` loop, so a raise there aborted exactly the same work. The critic's claim that "one bad key blocks more than it did" doesn't hold: the interleaving changes when locks are taken, not what a raise abandons. The test `test_a_raising_decision_releases_its_own_lock_and_every_kept_lock` asserts the current behavior.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: an exception while deciding one key's reload drops every restart and autostart in that batch until the next save
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: an exception while deciding one key's reload drops every restart and autostart in that batch until the next save
